content.text: Lesson 1 Overview

This lesson provides an introduction to renewable energy, emphasizing its role as a sustainable and abundant solution to global energy needs. The lesson highlights the economic advantages of renewable energy, including cost reductions and job creation, while addressing challenges like environmental impacts and resource extraction. Learners will gain an understanding of how renewable energy technologies are transforming global energy systems and contributing to a cleaner, more equitable future.

content.title: Part 1: Definition of Renewable Energy

content.text: These resources are considered sustainable because they are abundant and naturally occurring. In the other hand Fossil fuels, including coal, oil, and natural gas, are derived from ancient organic matter buried beneath the Earth's surface for millions of years. These fuels are extracted and burned to produce energy. Fossil fuels are considered non-renewable because their formation takes geological time scales that far exceed human lifespans. Once depleted, they cannot be replenished within a timeframe that aligns with global energy demands.

However, Renewable energy is not the same as clean energy. A wood fire is a renewable way to produce heat, but it also creates air pollution. And other energy sources, such as nuclear power, are clean but not renewable. But most energy sources that are eco-friendly are also renewable, and vice versa.
Note: Nuclear fuels, such as the element uranium, are not considered renewable as they are a finite material mined from the ground and can only be found in certain locations.

content.title: Part 2: Why Renewables?

content.text:
About 80 percent of the global population lives in countries that are net-importers of fossil fuels -- that’s about 6 billion people who are dependent on fossil fuels from other countries, which makes them vulnerable to geopolitical shocks and crises.
In contrast, renewable energy sources are available in all countries, and their potential is yet to be fully harnessed. The International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) estimates that 90 percent of the world’s electricity can and should come from renewable energy by 2050.
Renewables offer a way out of import dependency, allowing countries to diversify their economies and protect them from the unpredictable price swings of fossil fuels, while driving inclusive economic growth, new jobs, and poverty alleviation.
Sustainable

Renewable resources are naturally replenished and virtually inexhaustible on a human timescale, ensuring a continuous energy supply.

More Than 40% of World’s Electricity Came From Zero-Carbon Sources in 2023
Climate- Friendly

Utilizing renewable energy reduces greenhouse gas emissions and air pollutants, mitigating climate change and improving public health.


Fossil fuels are responsible for 75% of human-induced greenhouse gas emissions. In contrast, renewable energy sources produce minimal to no greenhouse gases during operation, significantly mitigating environmental impact. Only in 2022, renewable energy prevented over 1.7 gigatons of CO₂ emissions globally.
Unlimited Supply

Renewable energy sources like the sun, wind, and water do not run out. Unlike fossil fuels, they can keep producing energy indefinitely.


Solar and wind installations contributed to 80% of the new power capacity added globally in 2023.
Energy Independence

Countries that invest in renewable energy reduce their dependence on imported oil and gas, improving energy security.


For instance, Uruguay produced 98% of its electricity from renewables which significantly reduces its dependence on imported oil and gas and improving energy security.
Cost-Effective in the Long Run

Renewable energy actually is the cheapest power option in most parts of the world today. Prices for renewable energy technologies are dropping rapidly. The cost of electricity from solar power fell by 85 percent between 2010 and 2020. Costs of onshore and offshore wind energy fell by 56 percent and 48 percent respectively. Moreover, in 2023, 75% of new renewable energy installations were cheaper than the cheapest fossil fuel options.

Falling prices make renewable energy more attractive all around – including to low- and middle-income countries, where most of the additional demand for new electricity will come from. With falling costs, there is a real opportunity for much of the new power supply over the coming years to be provided by low-carbon sources.

Cheap electricity from renewable sources could provide 65 percent of the world’s total electricity supply by 2030. It could decarbonize 90 percent of the power sector by 2050, massively cutting carbon emissions and helping to mitigate climate change.

Although solar and wind power costs are expected to remain higher in 2022 and 2023 then pre-pandemic levels due to general elevated commodity and freight prices, their competitiveness actually improves due to much sharper increases in gas and coal prices, says the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Every dollar of investment in renewables creates three times more jobs than in the fossil fuel industry. The IEA estimates that the transition towards net-zero emissions will lead to an overall increase in energy sector jobs: while about 5 million jobs in fossil fuel production could be lost by 2030, an estimated 14 million new jobs would be created in clean energy, resulting in a net gain of 9 million jobs. For instance, the renewable energy industry employed over 13.7 million people globally in 2022.

In addition, energy-related industries would require a further 16 million workers, for instance to take on new roles in manufacturing of electric vehicles and hyper-efficient appliances or in innovative technologies such as hydrogen. This means that a total of more than 30 million jobs could be created in clean energy, efficiency, and low-emissions technologies by 2030.

Ensuring a just transition, placing the needs and rights of people at the heart of the energy transition, will be paramount to make sure no one is left behind.
Creates Jobs
Healthier

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), about 99 percent of people in the world breathe air that exceeds air quality limits and threatens their health, and more than 13 million deaths around the world each year are due to avoidable environmental causes, including air pollution.

The unhealthy levels of fine particulate matter and nitrogen dioxide originate mainly from the burning of fossil fuels. In 2018, air pollution from fossil fuels caused $2.9 trillion in health and economic costs, about $8 billion a day.

Switching to clean sources of energy, such as wind and solar, thus helps address not only climate change but also air pollution and health.

Despite significant role in reducing carbon emissions and multi-Dimensional benefits, renewable energy can have negative environmental impacts, if not managed well.

Large-scale solar farms and wind farms often require substantial land areas, potentially leading to habitat destruction and biodiversity loss. Improper siting of renewable energy infrastructure can disrupt local ecosystems and affect wildlife migration patterns. Additionally, the extraction of raw materials for renewable energy components contributes to land degradation and deforestation in mining regions. A circular economy approach that emphasizes resource efficiency and recycling can mitigate these impacts by reducing the demand for virgin materials and optimizing land use planning.

Intermittency is another major challenge for renewable energy sources like solar and wind, as their power generation depends on natural conditions that fluctuate—solar energy is limited to sunny hours, and wind turbines need sufficient wind speeds. This inconsistency can disrupt grid stability and requires significant investment in energy storage systems, such as batteries, to store excess energy for later use. Additionally, backup power systems, often fossil-fuel-based, are needed to fill gaps, reducing the net environmental benefits of renewables. While solutions like energy storage, grid upgrades, and diversification of energy sources are being developed, these come with high costs and technological demands, making intermittency a critical hurdle for scaling renewables globally.

content.title: Key Takeaways
content.intro: If you only have space to remember 3 things:

takeaways.title: Renewable energy is a cornerstone of addressing climate change and ensuring global energy security.
Transitioning to renewable energy enhances resilience, energy independence, and economic sustainability.
The cost of renewable energy has dropped significantly, making it a competitive and sustainable alternative to fossil fuels, while also creating millions of jobs worldwide.
